lesson.title: An Unlikely Champion: Lyndon B. Johnson and the Politics of Reform
lesson.summary: A masterful Senate dealmaker from Texas who became president after John F. Kennedy's assassination, Lyndon B. Johnson used his legislative skill to push through landmark civil rights and anti-poverty laws, even as the Vietnam War came to overshadow his presidency.
lesson.body:
Lyndon Baines Johnson became the thirty-sixth president of the United States on November 22, 1963, sworn in aboard Air Force One just hours after President Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas. A career politician from the Texas Hill Country, Johnson had served as Senate Majority Leader through much of the 1950s, where he became famous for a forceful, highly personal style of persuading colleagues, sometimes called the "Johnson Treatment," a skill he carried with him into the White House.

In the shock following Kennedy's death, Johnson moved quickly to push Kennedy's stalled civil rights bill through Congress, framing its passage as a way of honoring the fallen president's legacy. He drew on his deep Senate relationships and legislative know-how to help break the Southern filibuster, and he signed the Civil Rights Act into law on July 2, 1964.

Johnson won the 1964 presidential election in a landslide over his conservative Republican opponent, Barry Goldwater, giving him a strong mandate and a heavily Democratic Congress to pursue an ambitious domestic agenda he called the "Great Society," first outlined in a speech at the University of Michigan in May 1964. Over the following two years, he pushed through the Voting Rights Act, Medicare and Medicaid, federal aid to education, immigration reform, and much more.

His presidency was also defined, and ultimately undone, by the Vietnam War. Johnson escalated American military involvement dramatically after the Gulf of Tonkin incident and the congressional resolution that followed in August 1964, and U.S. troop levels in Vietnam rose sharply in the years after. Mounting casualties, a growing antiwar movement, and the enormous cost of the war strained public support and competed directly with the Great Society for funding and political attention.

Facing declining popularity and a divided Democratic Party, Johnson announced on March 31, 1968, that he would not seek reelection. His presidency stands as a study in contrast: some of the most significant civil rights and social welfare legislation of the twentieth century, achieved alongside a war that badly damaged his standing and the country's confidence in government.
